items.title: 'Pokémon' Leak Teases A Totally New Frontier For The Series
items.summary: After the explosive success of Palworld, Game Freak may feel pressure to develop a more ambitious type of Pokémon game after Winds and Waves
items.content:
By Patricia Hernandez Published Sep 22, 2026, 3:45 PM EDT Patricia is the former editor-in-chief of Kotaku , where she spent a decade writing and editing. Prior to that, she served as the Culture Editor at Polygon , and as a reporter at The Verge . Hernandez specializes in Pokémon TCG, Nintendo, and offbeat internet culture stories. News After the explosive success of Palworld, Game Freak may feel pressure to develop a more ambitious type of Pokémon game

Pokémon Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap From fighting games to MOBAs, the Pokémon series has experimented with nearly every type of video game genre. However, there's one specific genre that Pokémon has never officially attempted. It's a daunting genre that most gaming studios would never dare to try. Yet if recent rumors are true, Game Freak may soon defy expectations for the series — if not the wider gaming industry.

The rumor stems from an enormous leak suffered by series developer Game Freak back in 2025 , also known as the terraleak. Though leaks are becoming increasingly common in the world of video games , for the Pokémon brand, the breach was unprecedented. The terraleak contained a trove of internal documents that outlined a decade's worth of Pokémon video games, not just a single game. This included specific information on Pokémon Winds and Pokémon Waves that, at the time, hadn't been formally revealed by Game Freak.

One of those concepts included a game with the code name Project Seed. According to a leaked pitch deck describing the game, Project Seed was a digital recreation of Japan that combined multiple regions in the Pokémon universe into a single game. The series has tackled multiple regions before — famously, 1999's Pokémon Gold and Pokémon Silver opened up to the wider Kanto region after players cleared the Johto region.

The idea as described by internal Game Freak documents would allow players to seamlessly explore a persistent, real-time world together. The experimental project would include a range of biomes that spawn Pokémon based on location, weather, season, and time of day. The game would also reportedly focus on social interaction, though specific details on this aspect of the game were sparse.

News of Project Seed leaked in late 2025, alongside the rest of the Pokémon terraleak. The concept has reentered the news cycle because Pokémon leaker Centro discussed the project on social media recently. According to Centro, Game Freak has steadily been readying its fandom for an MMO-like experience. The franchise has already incorporated areas where players can see one another in real time, and tougher co-op raid encounters. Mass Outbreaks, which mimic limited world events, have been included in some shape or form since the second generation of Pokémon games.

What clues can we discern from looking at the back of Browt? Image: Game Freak/The Pokémon Company, Nintendo Other aspects of the rumor, like the emphasis on weather and location, are already evident in the mainline Pokémon games — including Winds and Waves . Nearly every modern Pokémon game has introduced regional variants. Yet some parts of the leak are dependent on other, as-of-yet unconfirmed Pokémon leaks. Per earlier reports, the tenth generation of Pokémon games will reportedly make evolutions more dynamic. Details like how a Pokémon is raised and the environment it is trained in are supposed to impact that monster's evolution. Pokémon that evolve this way are apparently called Seed Pokémon . If Seed Pokémon turn out to be real, a Game Freak project titled Project Seed that comes out after Winds and Waves makes perfect sense.

Would Pokémon truly attempt an MMO during a period when the gaming industry is shying away from live service games? Game Freak doesn't have a great track record for online connectivity in its games. Leakers also say that Project Seed may turn out to be a platform that other games build upon rather than its own distinct release.

Another potential wrinkle: All of these rumors are based on old documentation that may no longer be accurate. The chaotic nature of development makes it possible that all of these ideas were real at some point — yet they'll still never see the light of day. After the explosive success of Palworld , however, you have to imagine someone at Game Freak is mulling over how to push Pokémon into new territory. An MMO could be just the shake-up that the series needs.

A leaked UI may have a Moltres-themed tease as well as starter evolutions

items.title: Palworld lead thought one of Pocketpair's most iconic Pals would "fade into the background" before it unexpectedly became the survival game's "mascot"
items.summary: I never really thought Cattiva would be popular, like ever.
items.content:
"I never really thought Cattiva would be popular, like ever."

"For the record, this is my opinion," Buckley makes clear while chatting to Gaming World Interviews about the Pals who surprised him the most. "It's not the company's opinion. It's the opinion of me and me only. I never really thought Cattiva would be popular, like ever. Cattiva, Chikipi and Lamball were like the three-o in the beginning when you wake up on the beach."

Buckley goes on to say he was always "pretty confident" in Lamball, the adorably fluffy sheep-y creature who somehow looks even cuter holding a deadly weapon with a smile on its face. Chikipi and Cattiva, though? Buckley thought the duo would "fade into - not irrelevance, either - but fade into the background."

The Pocketpair lead acknowledges Chikipi has kind of "faded away" anyway. "It's a chicken, right?" But Cattiva? The pink smirking feline who always looks like it knows a secret it definitely won't share. "Cattiva is like the mascot."

Buckley explains that Cattiva and Chillet have slowly become some of the survival game's most recognizable faces, but Cattiva in particular is apparently "everywhere" in China. "There is a bit of regional difference with the Pals." If Cattiva was such an unexpected surprise, perhaps Pocketpair should return to the "graveyard" of scrapped Pal designs it never got around to finishing in the first place. You never know - there might be another seemingly horrendous creature the fanbase falls in love with, for some reason.

Palworld devs have "a graveyard" of scrapped Pals, but there was one they knew would be a hit Palworld was originally a "factory game like Satisfactory," lead says Palworld 1.0 redesigns multiple Pals and makes them look less like Pokemon As for 1.0 Pals, passion around Snock was a surprise to the lead dev. "Gamers are really into that snail or slug, whatever you want to call it."

Palworld Palfarm is less like Stardew Valley than you might expect, lead says, but it "is more on the cozier side" than Pocketpair's survival game

NPC at Fisherman’s Point in Mount Obsidian. “From the Far Side of the Moon” can be progressed after clearing “Beyond Dimensions.” ▼Pals and Skills ・Adjusted summoned Pals and Base Pals to prioritize notifications ・Added support for opening chat from the Radial Menu on PS5 ・Changed the default FPS cap to 120 on PC ・Version mismatch errors now show the version of the connection target ▼Performance World Tree area and other locations ▼Major Bug Fixes▼ ▼Crashes and Progression Issues ・Fixed an issue where controls could stop working after being returned to the title screen due to a connection Recent updates August 14, 2026: I've added a new base location for farming ore and coal in the early game. It's easily one of the best spots for both, and my new favorite place to set up in a fresh save.

(Image credit: Pocketpair) (Image credit: Pocketpair) Image 1 of 2 View Original

The Sunlit Isle (405, -483) Pros: Several crude oil nodes, easy to defend during raids Cons: No nearby ore Closest teleport: Sunlit Isle It's not the best spot for ore or stone, but the Sunlit Isle just east of Palworld's starting area makes early game crude oil farming a breeze with six nodes scattered across the land. It's not difficult to defend, and the pals living here are under level 10. I like building at the highest point along the island's south side, but there's a cute spot northeast with stone steps leading up to it that works just as well. Even if you intend to go elsewhere for ore farming, this is a great place to build a second base for a steady crude oil supply.

items.title: v1.0.3: Balance Adjustments & Bug Fixes
items.summary: \ Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released! ＝＝＝ \ ▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon. ・Changed the t
items.content:
\

Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released!

＝＝＝

\

▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon.

・Changed the technology unlock level of the Aquatic Construction Kit from Level 66 to Level 23, changed its Ancient Technology Point requirement from 4 to 1, and adjusted the required materials and work amount.

・Extended the duration of World Tree Holy Water.

・Reduced the weight of World Tree Holy Water from 1 to 0.1.

・Added World Tree Holy Water to the rewards for World Tree expeditions, World Tree fishing, and the Large Fishing Pond.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Pals in The World Tree area.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Teafant Spring.

・Adjusted the work amount required to craft the Ancient Armor series.

・Doubled the amount of Fiber obtained from trees.

▼Bases and Missions

・Reduced the building costs of the Crude Oil Extractor, High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor, and Large Power Generator.

・Increased the crude oil production speed of the Crude Oil Extractor and High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

・The base mission that requires building a Crude Oil Extractor can now also be progressed by building a High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

▼Server Settings

・Added a server setting (bAllowEnemyCampSpawnNearBaseCamp) that disables the suppression of enemy camp spawns near player base camps.

\

▼Graphics and Display

・Adjusted the boundary display in some areas to make it easier to see from a distance.

・Improved the display quality of some objects in dungeons.

▼Sound

・Added a sound effect when using World Tree Holy Water.

\

▼Crashes and Progression Blockers

・Fixed an issue where the mission could become impossible to progress if the barrier was removed before accepting the main mission in Sunreach.

▼Multiplayer and Co-op

・Fixed an issue in co-op where lighting on the client side could display incorrectly after cutscenes or the ending played.

・Fixed an issue in co-op where some scenes could stutter during the cutscene that plays when entering The World Tree.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Fast Travel could activate unintentionally during Tower Boss battles.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Pals could appear to vibrate rapidly on the client screen.

▼Pals and NPCs

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop fighting.

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop helping with base work.

・Fixed an issue in multiplayer where, when the Partner Skill of Orserk or certain other Pals activated, the effect display could fail to update correctly, making it appear as though the skill had not activated.

・Fixed an issue where Alpha Surfent would not produce Leather when assigned to a Ranch.

▼Battles and Bosses

・Fixed an issue where some raid boss battles could fail to progress as intended.

・Fixed an issue where the wave effect and actual damage range did not match for some of Panthalus's attacks.

▼Bases and Building

・Fixed an issue where the placement detection for stairs and slanted roofs could fail to match their actual shape.

・Fixed an issue where stairs could not be placed correctly on the sides of foundations or roofs.

▼Items and Rewards

・Fixed an issue where the reward settings for the normal Moon Lord battle and the Ultra Raid Boss battle had not been updated to the intended settings.

・Fixed an issue where items could duplicate when performing certain actions.

・Fixed an issue where, when Katress's Partner Skill activated, switching spheres while riding could allow the player to obtain a different type of sphere.

items.title: This New Survival Game Finally Clicked with Me, and I'm Never Looking Back
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 does a great job of easing you into its many complex systems.
items.content:
Survival games have been wildly popular for years now. I’ve dabbled here and there to see what the fuss is about, but I’ve always fallen off after a few hours. Usually, I get tangled up in one meagerly explained system after another until I lose track of what I’m supposed to do, and my time with the game peters out.

When Palworld 1.0 came out to rave reviews , I figured I’d give the genre another shot – and I’m glad I did. Palworld’s gradual, newbie-friendly onboarding helped me see what a whole lot of people have loved about survival games all along. Palworld made me a believer.

I’m glad I came in at the 1.0 mark, because I’ve heard Palworld had a much steeper learning curve out of the gate. But now, new players start with a series of missions designed to guide you through the game’s numerous systems . You learn how to punch trees to get wood to create a crafting bench. You learn how to make a club you can use to beat some Pals to death (it’s a dog-eat-dog world out there) to get wool. You then use that wool to make clothes. You set up a camp. You build a house. You activate a teleporter and explore deeper into the game world.

Before long, you’re gliding off cliffs Zelda-style before whomping on every Pal you see to catch them in spheres to put them to work. You can deploy them at your camp, ride them , or have them fight by your side to take on big roaming Pals and towering bosses . It’s a blast. And there’s no way I would have stuck with it if it hadn’t held my hand and eased me into the systems that make up the game.

I still have a long way to go, because I was nowhere near powerful enough to defeat the first boss solo. But those early missions gave me a much-needed handle on what else I can spend my time doing as I level up enough to become a threat. There's a vast world out there I can keep exploring, all while catching Pals and building up my base. I’m having a blast doing it.

Palworld’s 1.0 is available on Steam , Xbox , and PS5 . It costs $29.99, but you can save a few bucks on a Steam copy at Fanatical , which is currently running its summer sale .

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

items.title: I Stopped Playing Palworld For This Creature-Collector Game
Palworld 1.0 Review – Bigger, Better, and Still Brutally Addictive
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 is crammed with new content. More Pals, better quests, and a fully realized world for new and returning players to explore.
items.content:
Remember Palworld ? Well, the controversial game from Pocketpair finally has a 1.0 release. After two years, this feels like a very different animal than the one I initially encountered. The quest system is more complete, the UI is polished, and the world feels much more interconnected than before. While there are still some rough edges, this version of Palworld is a vastly improved one.

Now, I haven’t been keeping up with every iteration of Palworld released up to this point. So I’m not clear on how gradual or sudden these changes might be. But oh man, the quest system feels like night and day. You’re fed a steady stream of quests from the jump. They pair nicely with the tech tree, they appear on your map, and they sync with your compass. Yes, this is incredibly basic stuff. We figured out quest design decades ago. But you really appreciate the elegance of that design when it’s missing. Then when it finally shows up? It’s water in the desert.

Beyond the quests, it turns out Palworld works much better with connective tissue in place. Fast travel points, side quests, a detailed map, and distant objectives (like a floating island on the horizon) all make the world feel more tangible. Having an objective at all times kept me hooked on the game. Or at least, objectives are perfect for stringing you along until the factory sim element gets its claws in you. Once the big machine gets going, you don’t need anything else to maintain momentum.

The complete list of additions in Palworld 1.0 is downright intimidating. You can read the whole thing on their Steam page, but the highlights are remarkable. 72 new Pals, the Sunreach region, the World Tree, and an increased level cap all speak to a much larger, more complete game. There’s more of course, but the point remains – Palworld has undergone significant changes since the early access days.

This new version of Palworld still has some flaws, to be fair. The laptop I’m using is decently powerful, but I encountered a handful of framerate dips regardless. More important than the tiny performance issues is the core gameplay loop. Things hum along at a more relatable pace than ever before, sure. But you’re still faced with a pretty murderous grind. Pal levels creep upward slowly, and getting through that tech trees gets daunting quite quickly. While things start out breezy enough, the endgame is strictly for simulation psychopaths.

By which I mean the truly dedicated. Which is totally fine! There’s a fascinating disconnect between the monster battling and the base building. You can immerse yourself in one and ignore the other, at least for a hefty chunk of playtime. Although perhaps my impressions of the battling are skewed by hands off it all is. Your Pals run on autopilot, both in battle and beyond it. So for me, the fights are a diversion from my tiny empire.

In that regard, Palworld remains a specialized interest. Either you’re ready to get lost in the details of empire expansion and monster murder, or you’ll quickly lose momentum. The quest system, new content, and expanded Pal roster are all incidental in the face of this essential truth. The gooey caramel center that is the gameplay loop is more or less the same as it ever was. My mind was changed about this game, true. But I’m prone to hyper focus and bouts of mania. So a vast and ruthless machine like Palworld is straight up catnip for my badly wired brain.

The 1.0 release of Palworld presents a very different game than the original early access version. The quest system has been revamped, the map has been expanded, and civilization is scattered everywhere. But the gameplay loop is still pretty relentless. Plus, the rough edges haven’t been completely removed. If the old game was almost it for you, this new iteration might be exactly what you yearned for. But Palworld 1.0 is still an acquired taste.

***A Steam key was provided by the publisher***

} .login #login, .login #lostpasswordform { min-width: 350px !important; } .wpforms-field-c4wp iframe { width: 100% !important; } ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube Linkedin Palworld review: Fresh and innovative, despite appearances By Ryan Woodrow | July 22, 2026 Photo Credit: Pocketpair When Palworld first launched into early access two and a half years ago, I described it as a “breath of fresh air” for the survival-crafting genre, and in the time since then, the state of that genre hasn’t changed. I still find it to be one of the most stagnant genres out there, with a formula that I once found enjoyable when Minecraft and Terraria stumbled upon it, but has now been worn into the ground by every early access game on Steam.

That’s why I was so surprised how much creature collecting adds to that formula, but now the game has hit 1.0 and officially launched, I can see it goes a lot deeper than just slapping a couple hundred colorful creatures on top of the standard survival-crafting affair.

The Pals that roam the world aren’t just set dressing or collectibles; they’re integral to every single part of the core loop. Upon defeating or catching them, you get resources vital to progression that can’t be obtained through any other means; catching them is your main source of EXP, which is how you progress through the game’s tech tree; and most importantly, you can put the Pals to work at your base to complete tasks for you.

While the trailers for the game present this as a funny, edgy thing where they’re emphasizing the darker elements of the world that Pokémon likes to gloss over, putting Pals to work is a vital part of the game, and a surprisingly deep system.

There are 12 different work suitabilities that determine what tasks a Pal can perform. This includes things like planting, crafting, smelting, watering, and a bunch more, and each one has levels from 0 to 10 showing how quickly they’ll perform the task. This means that, as your base grows, finding the right balance of Pal proficiencies is vital to making meaningful progress, especially as, once you get out of the early game, there are many things that you won’t be able to do yourself.

Source: Pocketpair Take smelting, for example. You can’t just slap some coal in a furnace and wait for everything to cook; you have to get a fire Pal to cook it for you, and as you go up each tier of material, you’re going to need to find Pals that are much better at that task to get it done in a reasonable time frame.

And that’s all without taking into account the passive and partner skill systems, where every species of Pal has a unique partner skill, and every single Pal you catch has a random selection of passives that either help or hinder their work. It makes you actually care deeply about your Pals, as you’re paying attention to their every detail. While in Pokémon, you only have to worry about breeding and traits if you want to play competitively, in Palworld, that stuff is baked into the foundation of the singleplayer experience.

Not to mention, it also helps build the world, the lore, and the characters of the Pals. While some partner skills will be passive boosts, there are some Pal duos, like Anubis and Sehkmet, that specifically boost each other when working together, giving you another layer of considerations to make when organizing your base.

If that all sounds complicated, it really isn’t, as the game makes it very easy to manage. Early on, you’ll unlock a podium that lets you assign Pals to specific tasks, as well as dictate which of their proficiencies they are and aren’t allowed to use when unassigned, to ensure that everyone focuses on the jobs you intend for them.

But all of these Pals don’t just wander in unannounced; you have to seek them out in the world, which is Palworld’s other great strength: the exploration.

With an impressive draw distance, as soon as you walk out into the world, you’ll spot all kinds of wondrous sights. Volcanoes, snow mountains, lush forests, and even oil rigs all litter the landscape, and if you can see it, you can go there. The only restriction is the World Tree, which is locked behind endgame progression, but even that makes for a tantalizing mystery constantly on the horizon that you’re working towards.

Source: Pocketpair You settle into a well-paced loop where you work improving your base for a while, which in turn improves your gear so you can then go and explore further afield into higher-level areas with brand new Pals to catch, boosting your EXP and giving you new resources to help you progress even further when you return to base. It’s a simple loop, but one that so many survival-crafting games fail to implement satisfyingly; that’s the power of a creature collector.

So let’s talk about the Pals themselves, because with 204 unique designs and 278 total designs when you include hybrids – which are elemental variants on existing Pals that only vary in color – there are honestly very few misses among the pack. There are a handful of basic ones you probably won’t give much thought to, but the vast majority of Pals have a tangible charisma to their designs that makes them compelling.

I actually found the game’s five-Pal party quite restrictive considering how many cool designs there were that I wanted to use on my team, though this is where having many slots at your base for workers helps, as you do form relationships with those Pals too.

items.title: Palworld Has Now Outsold Almost Every Mainline Pokémon Game
items.summary: Palworld has reportedly sold 30.5 million copies, surpassing almost every mainline Pokémon game, including Scarlet and Violet
items.content:
Palworld has reportedly sold 30.5 million copies, surpassing almost every mainline Pokémon game, including Scarlet and Violet

X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount{ display:none; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount .discount-tag{ line-height: 24px !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button.most-popular .join-now-button:hover { background: #000 !important; color: #fff !important; outline: 1px solid #fff !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button:hover { background: 0 0; outline: 1px solid rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); color: rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); } @media (max-width: 1220px){ .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button { width: 100% !important; position: unset !important; } } A new report claims that Palworld has sold a staggering 30.5 million units. If accurate, Pocketpair’s controversial survival game has now outsold almost every mainline Pokémon release, including Scarlet and Violet , Sword and Shield , and Gold and Silver .

According to a new report from Alinea Analytics, Palworld has now sold an estimated 30.5 million units across Xbox, PlayStation, and PC . The video game market intelligence firm also estimates that Pocketpair has generated an eye-watering $700 million in total revenue following the recent launch of Palworld 1.0.

If these latest estimates are accurate, they also mean that Palworld has now significantly outsold many of the biggest Pokémon releases over the last 30 years. In Nintendo’s most recent financial report , for example, Pokémon Scarlet and Violet only sold a combined 28.08 million units on Nintendo Switch in comparison.

However, it’s bigger than that, as Palworld has also outsold most classic Pokémon generation titles such as Gold and Silver and Gen 4’s Diamond and Pearl . Here is a full breakdown of the sales figures:

Now, there are a few factors we need to point out here. Since its launch in 1996, the mainline Pokémon series has remained exclusive to Nintendo consoles. One major advantage Palworld has is that it’s an addictive creature-catcher available across most major gaming platforms.

Alinea Analytics points out that while Palworld generated most of its revenue on PC via Steam, it also sold millions of units on PlayStation 5. The game is additionally available on Xbox and through Game Pass, giving it access to a much larger potential audience than an individual Pokémon release.

However, while Palworld has many Pokémon games beat in terms of units sold, Nintendo’s series likely generates more revenue per copy. Pokémon games typically retail for $60 to $70 at launch, while Palworld originally entered early access for $29.99 and has frequently been discounted.

Finally, Nintendo does not update Pokémon sales figures every month, meaning Scarlet and Violet has almost certainly sold additional copies since its last reported total. It’s therefore possible that the Gen 9 games are closer to Palworld than the currently available figures suggest.

Regardless, selling an estimated 30.5 million copies is an incredible achievement for a new IP that only recently debuted in 2024. Palworld is now only around 880,000 units behind Pokémon Red, Green, and Blue , which remains the best-selling mainline Pokémon generation of all time.
